sentences.text: Leonerasaurus was a small non-sauropod sauropodomorph that displayed an unusual mix of primitive and advanced traits.
This animal measured approximately 2.40 meters in length, stood one meter high, and weighed about 70 kilograms.
The species is known from a single incomplete individual consisting of parts of the skull, teeth, vertebrae, hip and shoulder girdles, and limb bones.
The front teeth were spoon-shaped with a convex outer surface and a concave inner surface, resembling those of basal sauropods.
At least 15 teeth were present on one side of the lower jaw, and the tooth sockets were angled forward by approximately 60 degrees.
The sacrum, made of four fused vertebrae forming the center of the pelvis, is nearly complete, but no tail bones were recovered.
The unique combination of traits in Leonerasaurus suggests a high degree of convergent evolution in early sauropodomorphs.
Its forward-angled teeth are a feature similar to eusauropods and juvenile Mussaurus.
Leonerasaurus taquetrensis was named by Diego Pol, Alberto Garrido, and Ignacio A. Cerda in 2011.
Fossils of an incomplete juvenile individual were found near Cañadón Las Leoneras, southeast of Sierra de Taquetrén, in Chubut province, central Patagonia, Argentina.
The spoon-shaped front teeth with their specific curvature suggest a diet involving browsing or processing tough vegetation.
Leonerasaurus is classified as a basal genus of sauropodomorph dinosaur within the unranked group Anchisauria.

Research suggests Leonerasaurus belongs to the Anchisauria, appearing as the closest relative to the group containing sauropods and Melanorosaurus, though Melanorosaurus is considered a sauropod by some researchers.
The fossil of an incomplete subadult Leonerasaurus was found in the Early Jurassic Las Leoneras Formation in Argentina.
The Las Leoneras Formation is interpreted as dating from the Pliensbachian to Toarcian or late Sinemurian to Toarcian stages of the Early Jurassic.

Leonerasaurus taquetrensis lived approximately 190 million years ago during the Sinemurian stage of the Early Jurassic in what is now South America, with other estimates placing it between 192.9 and 184.2 million years ago during the Pliensbachian stage.

It is debated whether Leonerasaurus lived in the Late Triassic, as the lower age limit of the Las Leoneras Formation is not well-defined, and it is suggested that the evolution of primitive sauropodomorphs involved significant convergent evolution among diverse lineages.
